title: Random Local Stabilizer Codes in Three Dimensions without String or Self-Similar Fractal Logical Operators
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes (QECs) are essential components quantum computation and have deep connections to quantum phases of matter. A key obstruction to passive self-correcting QECs is the presence of string logical operators, which can generate logical errors through constant-energy-barrier processes. Haah's Codes (fracton codes) showed that three-dimensional stabilizer codes can forbid such string logical operators, but their translation-invariant structure supports self-similar fractal logical operators with a logarithmic energy barrier. We introduce the qutrit random cubic codes, a family of local qutrit Calderbank-Shor-Steane stabilizer Hamiltonians with similar cube-check structure as Haah's Code 1 but built from spatially varying stabilizers. We prove that these models retain the no-string property and numerically observe that they have properties distinct from translation-invariant fracton codes: the smallest ground-state degeneracy exponent is $k=2$ for odd $L$ and $k=4$ for even $L$; noncontractible plane-logical operators span the entire logical space; and charge-push diagnostics show that the self-similar fractal operators are absent. These results demonstrate that constrained randomness can fundamentally change the nature of stabilizer codes and improve their self-correction properties. They further point to broader families of quantum error-correcting codes and quantum phases beyond canonical topological and fracton orders.
summary: This paper introduces qutrit random cubic codes ($	ext{QtRCC}$) as an alternative to traditional topological QECs. By adapting complex geometric proofs from Haah's work to the qutrit setting, the authors prove that $	ext{QtRCC}$ remains free of string logical operators while simultaneously eliminating the self-similar fractal operators found in uniform models. This demonstrates that constrained randomness can yield novel and potentially superior quantum error-correcting phases.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop robust Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECs) that are passive self-correcting, specifically by proving the absence of string logical operators in three dimensions.
main_result: The proposed qutrit random cubic codes ($	ext{QtRCC}$) retain the no-string property and exhibit distinct properties from translation-invariant fracton codes, suggesting improved self-correction capabilities via constrained randomness.
method: The authors employ rigorous algebraic proofs by adapting geometric techniques (like corner/edge erasing) used in Haah's original work to the qutrit ($\mathbb{F}_3$) setting. They also use numerical diagnostics like charge-push protocols and GSD calculations.
model_or_system: The system is a family of local qutrit Calderbank-Shor-Steane stabilizer Hamiltonians defined on a cubic lattice, generalizing Haah's Code 1 structure but incorporating spatially varying stabilizers (QtRCC).
key_observables: Ground-state degeneracy exponent ($k$), minimum weight of plane-supported logical operators ($	ext{w}_{\min}$), and the absence of fractal recurrence in charge-push diagnostics.
important_parameters: The lattice size $L$, the qutrit nature ($\mathbb{Z}_3$ coefficients), and the parity dependence of the GSD exponent ($k=2$ for odd $L$, $k=4$ for even $L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the random models are sampled only from the 'admissible set' defined by global stabilizer relations and local commutation constraints, and that all relevant coefficients are nonzero.
figures_summary: Figures compare the ground-state degeneracy exponent ($k$) between uniform (QtHC) and random (QtRCC) codes, showing a stable parity pattern for QtRCC. They also visually demonstrate the absence of power-of-three fractal recurrence in charge-push diagnostics for QtRCC compared to QtHC.
paper_structure: The paper builds logically by first establishing the necessary algebraic framework for qutrit checks, then proving the no-string theorem via geometric reduction (corner/edge erasing), and finally using numerical diagnostics (plane scans, charge-push) to confirm the absence of fractal operators and characterize the resulting topological order.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete example of how introducing controlled randomness into highly structured quantum codes can fundamentally alter their underlying physical properties, moving beyond purely translation-invariant models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Local cube-check structure for Qutrit Random Cubic Codes (QtHC). The left panel shows the Z-check Ar and the right panel shows the reflected X-check Br. Each cube corner carries two qutrits, and the corresponding operators are displayed. With the corner convention of Eq. (4), the Z-check has no support at O and two-qutrit support at G, while the X-check has two-qutrit support at O and no support at G. The remaining six corners are one-operator corners.

FIG. 2. Example of an admissible Z-check coefficient field. The figure shows the z = 0 slice of the curated L = 10 exam- ple L10_model_01 [60]. Each square is one cube anchor and contains a compact glyph for the eight nonzero coefficients (w1, w2, uD, uE, uF , vA, vB, vC) of the local Z-check. Blue de- notes the finite-field value 1 ∈F3, and orange denotes 2 ∈F3. With translation invariance along the [111] direction, this plot defines the stabilizer code unambiguously.

FIG. 3. Schematic of the no-string proof strategy. A large connected support has stabilizer-violation regions shown as red cubes. Corner and good-edge erasing deform the rep- resentative to an axis-aligned corridor connecting the same endpoint charges. Further erasing gives the two flat rectangles. The confusing constraint then removes rows from the exposed edges: the white erased interval is longest on the outer row and shortens row by row as the induction moves inward, even- tually cutting the flat segment open if it is sufficiently long. The disconnected representative contradicts nontriviality of a sufficiently long fixed-width logical string segment.

FIG. 4. Ground-state degeneracy k = log3 GSD comparison for 10 ≤L ≤25. The translation-invariant QtHC reference model exhibits arithmetic finite-size fluctuations, including the large spike k = 54 at L = 18. The retained minimal- degeneracy QtRCC collection follows the parity pattern of Eq. (22), with k = 2 for odd L and k = 4 for even L.

FIG. 5. Example plane-supported X logical representative for the curated QtRCC example L10_model_01 [60]. The left panel gives a three-dimensional view of the operator support on the plane x = 0, and the right panel shows the same support projected to the transverse y-z plane. Blue markers denote first-qutrit factors XI, green markers denote second-qutrit factors IX, and the two shades distinguish exponents 1 and 2 in F3. This selected quotient-basis representative has weight 120: it occupies 90 of the 102 lattice sites in the plane, with 30 sites carrying both qutrit factors.
